prompt: Match each failure to the defence the lesson gives for it.
What do the three failures in this lesson have in common?
hint: Which part of TLS do they touch?

choices.text: Each one breaks the encryption algorithm itself
choices.why: The cryptography is left untouched in all three.

choices.text: They go around a weak setup
choices.why: Right. The cryptography is untouched; the setup is what fails.

choices.text: They need the attacker to hold the server's private key
choices.why: None of the three needs the key.

choices.text: They work from anywhere on the internet
choices.why: The attacker has to be on the path.

prompt: curl --tls-max 1.1 on laptop failed with exit 35, no protocols available. What does that tell you about the shop's server?

choices.text: That the server rejects TLS 1.1
choices.why: The server was never asked.

choices.text: That the server supports only TLS 1.3
choices.why: It also answered with TLS 1.2.

choices.text: Nothing: the client refused before the server was asked
choices.why: Right. It protects this client and proves nothing about the server.

choices.text: That the server's certificate is too old for TLS 1.1
choices.why: No certificate was exchanged.

prompt: With the client's floor lowered on purpose, the server refused TLS 1.1. What SSL alert number did it send?
Of the two mechanisms that close a downgrade, which one does an administrator control with one line?
hint: The shop's proxy has it on line 15.

choices.text: TLS 1.3's marker in the server random
choices.why: That is built into TLS 1.3, not configured.

choices.text: Making the server prefer TLS 1.3 while keeping TLS 1.0 enabled for old clients
choices.why: A downgrade needs acceptance, not preference.

choices.text: Removing old versions, as ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3 does
choices.why: Right. Nothing is left to downgrade to.

choices.text: Renewing the certificate
choices.why: The certificate does not choose the version.

prompt: A server prefers TLS 1.3 and still accepts TLS 1.0. Why is it exposed to a downgrade?

choices.text: A connection settles on the weakest version both sides tolerate
choices.why: Right. Accepting is enough; preferring does not matter.

choices.text: TLS 1.3 is disabled whenever 1.0 is on
choices.why: Both can be on together.

choices.text: It is not: preferring 1.3 closes the gap
choices.why: A downgrade does not need the server to prefer the old version.

choices.text: TLS 1.0 has no certificates
choices.why: It does; its weaknesses are elsewhere.

prompt: Match each piece of ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384 to what it chooses.

pairs.right: the signature proving the certificate's key
the hash that derives the keys

prompt: The server's key is stolen next year. Which part of the suite keeps this year's recorded connections unreadable?

choices.text: SHA384
choices.why: The hash derives keys; it does not make them fresh.

choices.text: GCM, because it authenticates each record
choices.why: Authentication refuses changes; it does not protect past keys.

choices.text: ECDSA, because it signs with the certificate's key
choices.why: That key is the one stolen.

choices.text: The E in ECDHE: a fresh key per connection
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Which of these should a server refuse to offer? Choose all that apply.
hint: The list of what to refuse.

choices.text: RSA key exchange
choices.why: Right. No forward secrecy.

choices.text: CHACHA20-POLY1305
choices.why: It is authenticated encryption, on the list to require.

choices.text: 3DES
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: CBC-mode suites
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: ECDHE key agreement
choices.why: It is what gives forward secrecy.

prompt: How many seconds of max-age did the shop's Strict-Transport-Security header promise?
The shop redirects plain HTTP with a 301 to HTTPS. Why does that redirect alone not stop stripping?

choices.text: A 301 is cached, so it is sent once
choices.why: Caching is not the problem here.

choices.text: The first request and the redirect travel in clear
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Browsers ignore a redirect that switches from HTTP to HTTPS
choices.why: They follow them.

choices.text: The Location header is encrypted
choices.why: It travels in clear; that is the problem.

prompt: A browser that has never visited the site before. What keeps even its first request off plain HTTP?

choices.text: The Strict-Transport-Security header on the HTTPS answer
choices.why: That arrives after the first visit.

choices.text: The 301 redirect
choices.why: It follows a request in clear.

choices.text: The HSTS preload list
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: includeSubDomains in the header
choices.why: It widens the header, which a first visit has not seen.

prompt: After the header with includeSubDomains went out, staff say the old intranet at http://wiki.example.com stopped opening. Why?
hint: What did the header commit to?

choices.text: The proxy now redirects wiki's traffic to the shop
choices.why: The redirect is only in the shop's server block.

choices.text: HSTS closes port 80 on every server in the domain
choices.why: It is a browser rule, not a firewall.

choices.text: The wiki's certificate expired
choices.why: It is on plain HTTP; it has none.

choices.text: Browsers that saw the header use HTTPS for subdomains too
choices.why: Right. A plain-HTTP subdomain stops working in them.

prompt: Deploy Strict-Transport-Security with a short ___ first, and raise it to a year once nothing broke.
hint: The directive that sets the duration.

prompt: The impostor's certificate says CN = www.example.com, the right name. Why did curl still refuse it?

choices.text: It is self-signed: nothing the client trusts vouches for it
choices.why: Right. Subject and issuer are the same.

choices.text: Port 8443 is not a port that browsers and curl accept for HTTPS
choices.why: The port is not what the check looks at.

choices.text: Its name does not match
choices.why: The name matches.

choices.text: It uses TLS 1.1
choices.why: The error was self-signed certificate.

prompt: What Verify return code did openssl s_client print for the impostor's certificate?
With -k, curl printed 200 from 203.0.113.50. What happened to that connection?

choices.text: It was sent in clear
choices.why: It was encrypted.

choices.text: It reached the real shop, since the page loaded
choices.why: 203.0.113.50 is remote, not the shop.

choices.text: Encrypted, to the wrong machine
choices.why: Right. Anything sent went to whoever runs remote.

choices.text: It was encrypted but its contents were signed by a CA the client trusts
choices.why: No CA vouched for anything.

prompt: Match each place to the setting that turns certificate verification off there.
The search for insecure spellings on laptop printed matches: 1. What does that mean?

choices.text: One insecure line was found
choices.why: It is the exit status, not a count.

choices.text: grep failed to read the directory
choices.why: That would be exit 2.

choices.text: Nothing matched
choices.why: Right. grep exits 1 when nothing matched.

choices.text: Only the Python files were searched and one matched
choices.why: Shell and Go files were searched as well.

prompt: fetch.py printed CERT_REQUIRED and check_hostname: True. What do those two settings check between them?
hint: The two halves of the check.

choices.text: The TLS version and the cipher suite
choices.why: Those are negotiated, not verified here.

choices.text: The chain to a trusted authority, and the name
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: That the server sent a Strict-Transport-Security header
choices.why: HSTS is a browser rule.

choices.text: That the certificate uses ECDSA
choices.why: The key type is not checked.

prompt: Order the steps to put HSTS on a site that is today served over plain HTTP, from first to last.
hint: Short promise before a long one.
items: serve the site over HTTPS and redirect plain HTTP to it
add Strict-Transport-Security with a short max-age
raise max-age to a year once nothing broke
submit the domain to the HSTS preload list
trap: Preloading before the header has been tested commits every browser to a promise nothing checked.

prompt: A review finds InsecureSkipVerify: true in a Go client that talks to an internal service with a self-signed certificate. What is the fix?

choices.text: Keep it, since the service is internal
choices.why: Traffic inside can arrive at the wrong machine too.

choices.text: A certificate from the company's CA, and its root in the client's trust store
choices.why: Right. Then remove the flag.

choices.text: Restrict the client to TLS 1.3
choices.why: A newer version does not validate the certificate.

choices.text: Add an HSTS header to the internal service
choices.why: HSTS is for browsers and does not validate anything.

prompt: On café Wi-Fi, a user who has visited the shop before types www.example.com. The shop sends HSTS. Which of the three failures is already closed for this user?
hint: The browser saw the header before.

choices.text: Downgrade, since HSTS forbids TLS 1.1
choices.why: HSTS is about HTTP versus HTTPS, not TLS versions.

choices.text: No validation, since HSTS checks the certificate
choices.why: The client's certificate check does that.

choices.text: None of them, since the café's network is untrusted
choices.why: The browser refuses plain HTTP before sending.

choices.text: Stripping
choices.why: Right. No clear request goes out to be answered.
